fields.title: Joshua
fields.subtitle: Yehoshua, “The LORD saves”
fields.description: The book that carries Israel across the Jordan, named after the man who led them, whose name means “the LORD saves”. It opens at Moses’ death with a charge, “Be strong and courageous”, and closes at Shechem with a choice: “My household and I will serve the LORD.” Between the two: Rahab and the scarlet cord, the river stopped in a single heap and twelve stones set up for children to ask about, the walls of Jericho, Achan’s buried plunder, a sun that stood still at Gibeon, old Caleb asking for the hill country of the giants, the land shared out tribe by tribe, and a God of whom it is said that not one of his good promises failed. In the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Hebrew given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the book’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the book of Joshua about?
qa.answer: Israel’s entry into the land God had promised to Abraham, under Moses’ successor Joshua. Chapters 1–12 tell of the crossing of the Jordan, the fall of Jericho, the defeat and victory at Ai, the treaty with Gibeon and the campaigns in the south and north; chapters 13–21 tell how the land was divided among the twelve tribes; and chapters 22–24 close with Joshua’s farewell and the covenant renewed at Shechem. Its theme is summed up in 21:45: of all the good promises the LORD had made to Israel, not one failed.

qa.question: Who wrote the book of Joshua, and when?
qa.answer: The book does not name its author. An old Jewish tradition holds that Joshua wrote most of it, with the account of his death completed by others. Many scholars see it as part of a longer history running from Deuteronomy to Kings that reached its final form centuries later; its repeated phrase “to this day” shows a writer looking back on the events. Christians also differ over when the conquest took place, some dating it to the fifteenth century BC and others to the thirteenth.

qa.question: Who was Rahab in the Bible?
qa.answer: A Canaanite woman of Jericho, a prostitute, who hid Joshua’s two spies and confessed that “the LORD your God is God in heaven above and on earth below” (2:11). She tied a scarlet cord in her window, and when the city fell her whole household was spared (6:25). The New Testament honours her three times: as a hero of faith in Hebrews 11:31, as an example of faith shown in action in James 2:25, and as an ancestor of Jesus in Matthew 1:5.

qa.question: How should Christians read the violence in Joshua?
qa.answer: With care, and Christians answer the question in more than one way. Many stress that the Bible presents the conquest as God’s judgement on the long wickedness of the peoples of Canaan (Genesis 15:16; Deuteronomy 9:5); some note that ancient war reports used sweeping language of total victory, while Joshua itself records that many Canaanites remained; others point out that Rahab and the Gibeonites were spared and that the same judgement fell on Israel’s own Achan. Christians today broadly agree, though the book has sometimes been misused to justify violence, that it describes a unique moment in the history of God’s promise and gives no warrant for violence in God’s name today.

qa.question: What does Joshua mean by “My household and I will serve the LORD”?
qa.answer: It is Joshua’s declaration at the covenant gathering at Shechem near the end of his life (24:15), familiar from older Bibles as “as for me and my house”. Having retold all God had done for Israel, Joshua calls the people to choose between the LORD and the gods their ancestors had served, and states his own choice for his whole family. The people promise to serve the LORD, and Joshua writes the covenant down and sets up a stone as a witness.

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. “LORD” in capitals stands for God’s personal name. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Hebrew beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
Have I not given you this command? Be strong and courageous. Do not tremble with fear or lose heart, for the LORD your God is with you wherever you go.”

— Joshua 1:9

The book of Joshua opens at a graveside. Moses, who had led Israel out of Egypt and through forty years in the wilderness, has died on a mountain looking across the Jordan into a land he would never enter. The people are camped on the eastern bank. The river is in flood. And the first words God speaks are blunt: “My servant Moses is dead. Now get up and cross this Jordan.”

What follows is the story of a promise coming true. Four centuries earlier God had told Abraham that his descendants would have this land. Joshua tells how they crossed into it, how they fought for it, how it was shared out among the tribes, and how, at the end of his life, Joshua gathered the people and asked them to choose whom they would serve. It also raises one of the hardest questions in the Bible, which this introduction will not pretend is easy.

“The LORD saves”

The book is named after its central figure. Joshua son of Nun first appears in Exodus as Moses’ young assistant, fighting the Amalekites and waiting on the mountain while Moses meets with God. He was one of the twelve men sent to explore Canaan, and one of only two, with Caleb, who came back saying that the LORD could give them the land. Numbers records that Moses changed his name: “Moses gave Hoshea son of Nun the name Joshua.” Hoshea means “salvation”; Yehoshua adds the name of God, and means “the LORD saves”.

In Greek, Yehoshua becomes Iēsous, Jesus, and the letter to the Hebrews says that the rest Joshua gave was not the last word: “If Joshua had brought them into rest, God would not afterward speak of a different day.” Christians from the second century on (the Epistle of Barnabas, Justin Martyr) have seen in Joshua a picture of the greater Joshua, who leads his people into an inheritance no one can take away.

The shape of the book

Joshua falls into three parts.

  • Entering and taking the land (chapters 1–12). The charge to Joshua, Rahab and the spies, the crossing of the Jordan, the camp at Gilgal, the fall of Jericho, Achan’s sin and the defeat at Ai, the covenant renewed at Mount Ebal, the treaty with Gibeon, and the campaigns in the south and north, ending with a list of thirty-one defeated kings.
  • Dividing the land (chapters 13–21). The boundaries and towns given by lot to each tribe, Caleb’s request for Hebron, the cities of refuge, and the towns for the Levites.
  • Holding the land (chapters 22–24). An altar beside the Jordan that nearly starts a civil war, Joshua’s farewell to the leaders, and the great covenant at Shechem.

The middle section, with its lists of borders and villages, is the part most readers skip. But it is the point of the whole: the promise to Abraham was not a war but a home.

Be strong and courageous

The first chapter sounds one phrase four times. God says it to Joshua three times, and at the end of the chapter the people say it back to him: “Only be strong and courageous!” It is the courage of a man taking up a task too big for him, and it rests on a promise: “I will be with you just as I was with Moses. I will not let go of you or abandon you.” The letter to the Hebrews would later give that same promise to every believer.

The courage is also tied to a book. He is told to keep the law Moses gave:

Keep this book of the law always on your lips, and reflect on it by day and by night, so that you take care to do all that is written in it. Then you will bring your ways to a good end, and then you will act wisely and succeed.

— Joshua 1:8

Success in the land will come, not from military skill, but from listening to God’s word and doing it. The book ends on the same note.

Rahab and the scarlet cord

The first person in the land to confess faith in Israel’s God is a Canaanite: Rahab, a prostitute of Jericho, who hides Joshua’s two spies under flax stalks on her roof and sends the king’s men off on a false trail. Then she tells the spies why:

When we heard it, our hearts melted, and no one had any courage left because of you, for the LORD your God is God in heaven above and on earth below.

— Joshua 2:11

She has heard what the LORD did at the Red Sea, and she has drawn the right conclusion. She asks the spies to swear that, since she has shown them “faithful love”, they will show it to her family. They tell her to tie a scarlet cord in the window, and when the city falls, everyone inside her house is spared.

Rahab’s story is told with remarkable care, at the very moment the book is describing a people under judgement. She is the first sign that the line between those who are saved and those who are not runs through faith, not through race. The New Testament remembers her three times: Hebrews names her among the heroes of faith, James as an example of faith shown in deeds, and Matthew’s Gospel places her in the family line of Jesus, as the mother of Boaz. Many Christian writers, from Clement of Rome onward, have seen in the scarlet cord a sign of the blood of Christ, as the Passover blood once marked the doors in Egypt.

Crossing the Jordan

Israel had left Egypt through the sea. Now they enter Canaan through a river, and the book tells it deliberately as a second crossing. The priests carry the ark of the covenant ahead of the people; as soon as their feet touch the water, the flow from upstream stops and rises “in a single heap”, and the whole nation crosses “on dry ground”.

Joshua has twelve men take twelve stones from the riverbed and set them up at Gilgal, the first camp in the land. The reason is the next generation:

Then he said to the Israelites, “In time to come, when your children ask their parents, ‘What do these stones mean?’ then explain it to your children: ‘Israel crossed this Jordan on dry ground.’

— Joshua 4:21–22

Faith in Joshua is something handed on, to children not yet born, and beyond them, “so that all the peoples of the earth may know how mighty the hand of the LORD is.”

Gilgal: before the battle

Before a single battle is fought, the book slows down. At Gilgal the men born in the wilderness receive circumcision, the covenant sign, and the LORD says, “Today I have rolled away from you the disgrace of Egypt.” They keep the Passover. And the manna, the bread from heaven that had fed them every morning for forty years, stops: “that year they ate from the crops of the land of Canaan.” The wilderness is over.

Then, near Jericho, Joshua meets a man with a drawn sword and asks the question any general would ask: “Are you on our side, or on the side of our enemies?” The answer turns the question round:

“Neither,” he answered. “I am the commander of the army of the LORD, and now I have come.” Then Joshua threw himself down with his face to the ground and bowed low. He said to him, “What does my lord wish to say to his servant?”

— Joshua 5:14

The stranger tells him to take off his sandals, as Moses was told at the burning bush. The question is never whether God is on Israel’s side, but whether Israel is on God’s.

Jericho and Ai

The fall of Jericho is the most famous story in Joshua, and the strangest military plan in history. For six days the army marches once around the city in silence, with seven priests blowing ram’s horns before the ark. On the seventh day they go around seven times, the horns sound, the people shout, “and the wall collapsed where it stood.” The city is not taken. It is given.

Then Israel is beaten at Ai, a small town, because of one man. Achan has taken from Jericho what was set apart for God, and his confession is the oldest pattern of temptation there is: “I saw… I coveted them and took them, and now they are buried in the ground in the middle of my tent.” The whole people suffers for one man’s hidden sin, and Achan and his household are put to death in the Valley of Achor, “Trouble”. It is a hard chapter: the people of God are bound together, and what one member hides affects them all. Centuries later the prophet Hosea heard God promise to “make the valley of Achor a door of hope.”

When Ai is finally taken, Joshua does something unexpected. He leads the whole nation to Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim, as Moses had commanded, builds an altar, and reads the law aloud: “There was not a single word of all that Moses had commanded that Joshua did not read aloud before the whole assembly of Israel, including the women and children and the outsiders who lived among them.”

The hard question: “devoted to destruction”

No honest reader can pass over the violence in Joshua. Again and again the book says that a city and its people were “devoted to destruction”: men and women, young and old. The Hebrew word, herem, means something set apart wholly to God, given up to him and not to be kept for human use. In war it meant total destruction. Many readers find it the most troubling thing in the Old Testament.

Christians have answered it in more than one way, and it is fair to set them side by side. Many have stressed that the Bible presents this as God’s judgement on the long-standing wickedness of the peoples of Canaan, delayed for centuries because, as God told Abraham, “the Amorites’ wickedness has not yet run its full course”; and that Deuteronomy insists Israel was given the land not because it was righteous. Some have noted that the language of total victory was common in ancient war reports, and that the book itself tells, in the same breath, of Canaanites who remained, so that its sweeping summaries may not be meant as a literal count. Others have pointed out that the same judgement turns on Israel when Achan sins, and that Rahab and the Gibeonites, Canaanites both, are spared.

On one point Christians today broadly agree, though the book has sometimes been misused to justify violence. The book describes a particular event in the history of God’s promise, under a particular command, at a particular time. It gives no warrant to anyone, ever, to take up arms in the name of God against a people. The New Testament reads its battles as pictures of a different warfare, and its promised rest as one that Christ gives.

The Gibeonites and the long day

Chapter 9 tells of a different kind of defeat. The people of Gibeon, a Canaanite city, disguise themselves as travellers from far away in worn-out sandals with dry, crumbling bread, and ask for a treaty. Israel’s leaders inspect the bread, “but they did not seek the word of the LORD”, and they swear an oath. When the trick is discovered, Israel keeps its word, and the Gibeonites become woodcutters and water carriers for the sanctuary. A promise made in God’s name, even to the wrong people, must be kept.

And it is kept at once, at some cost. When five kings attack Gibeon for making peace with Israel, Joshua marches all night to defend them. That is the setting for the long day, when Joshua prays, “Sun, stand still at Gibeon, and moon, in the valley of Aijalon!” The book quotes an old poem from the Book of Jashar and then gives its own verdict:

No day before it or after it has been like it, a day when the LORD listened to a man’s voice in this way. Truly the LORD fought for Israel.

— Joshua 10:14

Readers differ over what happened in the sky that day: a day miraculously lengthened, or the language of battle-song. Either way, the book’s wonder is not the sun but the God who listened.

Dividing the land

From chapter 13 the battles give way to boundaries, shared out by lot at Gilgal and then at Shiloh, where the tent of meeting is set up. Some things stand out.

The first is Caleb. At eighty-five he comes to Joshua and reminds him that forty-five years earlier the two of them alone had trusted God when the other spies spread fear. “Today I am just as strong as on the day Moses sent me,” he says, and asks for the hill country of Hebron, where the giants lived, because “Perhaps the LORD will be with me, and I will drive them out.” Three times the book says that Caleb followed the LORD “with all his heart”.

The second is the tribe of Levi, which receives no territory at all: “The LORD, the God of Israel, is their inheritance.” The third is the six cities of refuge, where someone who had killed a person by accident could flee and be safe from revenge until a fair hearing.

The fourth is a quiet, persistent refrain: “But the people of Judah could not drive out the Jebusites”; “they never drove them out completely.” The conquest is real, but it is not finished. God tells the aging Joshua that “very much of the land still remains to be taken.” And yet the section closes with one of the great summary sentences of the Bible:

Of all the good promises the LORD had made to the house of Israel, not one failed; every one of them was fulfilled.

— Joshua 21:45

Both are true at once: God has kept every word, and his people have not yet taken hold of all he has given. Believers have lived between those two sentences ever since.

An altar called Witness

In chapter 22 the tribes east of the Jordan build a large altar by the river, and the other tribes, fearing apostasy, gather for war. But the altar was never meant for sacrifice. It was a reminder, so that their children would never be told “You have no share in the LORD.” War is avoided because someone asked before they struck.

Choose today

The book ends with two farewell speeches. In the first, Joshua, “old and well along in years”, reminds the leaders that “not a single word has fallen short of all the good words the LORD your God spoke about you”, and warns them that the God who has kept his promises of good will keep his warnings too.

In the second, at Shechem, where Abraham had built his first altar in the land, Joshua tells the whole story again, from Terah serving other gods beyond the River, through the patriarchs and Egypt and the wilderness, to the gift of “a land you had not worked for and towns you had not built”. Then he puts the question to them:

If serving the LORD seems wrong to you, then make your choice today. Whom will you serve? The gods your ancestors served beyond the River, or the gods of the Amorites, whose land you now live in? My household and I will serve the LORD.”

— Joshua 24:15

The people answer at once that they will serve the LORD. Joshua replies: “You will not be able to serve the LORD, because he is a holy God, a jealous God.” He is making sure they know what they are promising. Three times they insist, and Joshua writes the covenant down, sets up a great stone under the oak by the sanctuary, and sends them home, each to their inheritance.

How to read Joshua

Read the story chapters (1–12, 22–24) straight through first, then go back to the land lists in chapters 13–21 with a map beside you. Watch for the phrases that recur: “be strong and courageous”, “to this day”, “the LORD fought for Israel”, the stones set up as memorials at the Jordan, at Achor, at Ai and at Shechem.

The book does not name its author. An old Jewish tradition holds that Joshua wrote most of it, with the account of his death added by others. Many scholars see it as one part of a longer history running from Deuteronomy to Kings, shaped over time and completed later; its repeated note that things remain “to this day” shows a writer looking back. Christians also differ over the date of the events, some placing them in the fifteenth century BC and others in the thirteenth, and over how to read the archaeology of Jericho and other sites. None of these questions changes what the book is about.

Read Joshua as the hinge between Moses and the kings, between the promise and the history of a people in the land. And read it, as the New Testament does, as part of a larger story: a God who keeps his word, a rest that is given and then still awaited, and a leader named “the LORD saves” who points beyond himself.

About this translation

The text in this edition is the Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and given freely to the public domain. It is printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. A few of its choices in Joshua are worth knowing before you begin.

“The LORD.” Where the Hebrew uses God’s personal name, the four letters often written Yahweh, this translation follows long Jewish and Christian custom and writes “the LORD”. Where it uses the ordinary word for God, it writes “God”.

“Devoted to destruction.” The Hebrew herem, which older Bibles render “accursed” or “utterly destroyed”, is translated “devoted to destruction”, and the plunder that belonged to God “the devoted things”. The phrase keeps both sides of the word: something set apart for God, and something not to be kept.

“Faithful love” and “outsiders.” When Rahab asks the spies to show her family the kindness she has shown them, the word is hesed, translated here “faithful love”. And the foreigners who lived among Israel and heard the law read at Mount Ebal are called “outsiders”, people living as guests in a land not their own, as Israel itself had once lived in Egypt.

For the reasoning behind every sentence of the translation, with the Hebrew beside it, see the Open Word Bible itself at openwordbible.org.

fields.title: Joshua 1
fields.body_html:
Be strong and courageous

After the death of Moses, the servant of the LORD, the LORD spoke to Joshua son of Nun, Moses’ assistant. The LORD said, “My servant Moses is dead. Now get up and cross this Jordan, you and all these people, into the land I am about to give them, to the Israelites. I have given you every place where you set foot, just as I promised Moses. Your territory will reach from the wilderness to this Lebanon, and as far as the great river, the Euphrates, all the land of the Hittites, and west to the Great Sea where the sun sets. No one will be able to stand against you as long as you live. I will be with you just as I was with Moses. I will not let go of you or abandon you. Be strong and courageous, because you are the one who will lead this people to take as their inheritance the land I swore to their ancestors to give them. Only be strong and very courageous. Take care to keep the whole law that my servant Moses laid on you. Do not swerve from it to right or left, and then you will act wisely and succeed wherever you go. Keep this book of the law always on your lips, and reflect on it by day and by night, so that you take care to do all that is written in it. Then you will bring your ways to a good end, and then you will act wisely and succeed. Have I not given you this command? Be strong and courageous. Do not tremble with fear or lose heart, for the LORD your God is with you wherever you go.”

Get ready to cross the Jordan

So Joshua gave orders to the officials of the people: “Go through the camp and give the people this order: ‘Get your food ready for the journey, because three days from now you will cross this Jordan to go in and take possession of the land the LORD your God is giving you as your own.’”

The tribes east of the Jordan cross armed

Then Joshua spoke to the Reubenites, the Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh: “Remember the command that Moses the servant of the LORD gave you: ‘The LORD your God is giving you rest, and he will give you this land.’ Your wives, your children and your livestock may stay in the land Moses gave you east of the Jordan. But all your fighting men must cross over armed, going ahead of your fellow Israelites, and you must help them, until the LORD gives your fellow Israelites rest as he has given you, and they too take possession of the land the LORD your God is giving them. After that you may go back to the land that is yours and possess it, the land Moses the servant of the LORD gave you east of the Jordan, toward the sunrise.” They answered Joshua, “We will carry out all your orders to us, and we will go wherever you send us. We obeyed Moses in everything, and in the same way we will obey you. Only may the LORD your God be with you the way he was with Moses. Anyone who rebels against your orders and does not obey your words, whatever you command, will be put to death. Only be strong and courageous!”

fields.title: Joshua 2
fields.body_html:
Rahab hides the two spies

Then Joshua son of Nun secretly sent two men from Shittim to spy. “Go and look over the land,” he told them, “and Jericho above all.” So they set off and came to the house of a prostitute named Rahab, and they stayed the night there. The king of Jericho was told, “Some men from the Israelites have come here tonight to search out the land.” So the king of Jericho sent word to Rahab: “Bring out the visitors who came to you and went into your house. They have come to spy out the whole land.” But the woman had taken the two men and hidden them. “It is true, the men did come to me,” she said, “but I did not know where they came from. When the gate was about to be shut at dark, the men left. I do not know where they went. Go after them quickly. You will catch them.” In fact she had brought them up to the roof and covered them with the flax stalks she had spread out there. So the men set out after them along the road to the Jordan, as far as the river crossings, and as soon as the pursuers had gone out, the gate was shut. Before the men lay down to sleep, she came up to them on the roof and told them, “I know the LORD has given this land to you. Terror of you has fallen on us, and everyone who lives in the land is melting in fear before you. We have heard how the LORD made the water of the Red Sea dry up before you as you left Egypt. And we have heard how you dealt with the two Amorite kings across the Jordan, Sihon and Og: you devoted them to destruction. When we heard it, our hearts melted, and no one had any courage left because of you, for the LORD your God is God in heaven above and on earth below. So now, swear to me by the LORD: since I have shown you faithful love, you too will show faithful love to my father’s family. Give me a sign I can trust that you will keep my father and mother alive, with my brothers and sisters and all their people, and rescue us from death.” The men answered her, “We stake our lives on yours, even to death, so long as you do not tell anyone about our mission. When the LORD gives us the land, we will treat you with faithful love and keep our word.” Then she let them down by a rope through the window, because her house was built into the city wall; she lived in the wall itself. She told them, “Go to the hills, so that the men chasing you will not find you. Hide there for three days until they come back, and after that you can go on your way.” The men told her, “This oath you have made us swear will not bind us unless, when we come into the land, you tie this scarlet cord in the window you let us down through, and bring your father and mother, your brothers and all your father’s family into your house with you. Anyone who goes out through the doors of your house into the street will be responsible for their own death, and we will be free of blame. But if anyone who is with you in the house is harmed, the blame for their death will be on us. And if you tell anyone about our mission, we will not be bound by the oath you made us swear.” “Agreed,” she replied. “Let it be as you say.” She sent them on their way, and they left. Then she tied the scarlet cord in the window. So they went into the hills and stayed there three days, until the men chasing them had gone back. The pursuers had searched all along the road without finding them. Then the two men came back down from the hills, crossed the river and came to Joshua son of Nun. They told him everything that had happened to them. “The LORD has surely handed the whole land over to us,” they told Joshua. “Everyone who lives there is melting in fear because of us.”

fields.title: Joshua 3
fields.body_html:
Israel comes to the Jordan

Joshua got up early in the morning. He and all the Israelites set out from Shittim and came to the Jordan, and they stopped there for the night before crossing over. At the end of three days the officers went throughout the camp. They gave the people this order: “As soon as you see the Levitical priests carrying the ark of the covenant of the LORD your God, move out from where you are and follow it. But keep a distance of about 3,000 feet between yourselves and the ark; do not go near it. Then you will know which way to go, since you have never traveled this way before.”

Joshua told the people, “Set yourselves apart as holy, because tomorrow the LORD is going to work wonders among you.” Joshua said to the priests, “Take up the ark of the covenant and go across ahead of the people.” So they took up the ark of the covenant and went on ahead of the people.

I will be with you as I was with Moses

Then the LORD said to Joshua, “Today I will begin to raise you up in the sight of all Israel, so that they will know I will be with you as I was with Moses. Now you are to give an order to the priests who carry the ark of the covenant: ‘Once you have reached the edge of the Jordan’s waters, stop and stand in the river.’”

The waters of the Jordan stop

Joshua said to the Israelites, “Come over here and listen to the words of the LORD your God.” Joshua went on, “Here is the way you will know that the living God is in your midst, and that he will without fail drive out ahead of you the Canaanites, Hittites, Hivites, Perizzites, Girgashites, Amorites, and Jebusites. See, the ark of the covenant of the Lord of all the earth is going ahead of you into the Jordan. Now choose twelve men from the tribes of Israel, one man from each tribe. The priests carrying the ark of the LORD, the Lord of all the earth, will set the soles of their feet in the Jordan’s waters, and as soon as they do, the waters of the Jordan will be cut off. The water flowing down from upstream will stand up in a single heap.” So when the people broke camp to cross the Jordan, with the priests carrying the ark of the covenant ahead of them, and as soon as the men carrying the ark reached the Jordan and the priests’ feet dipped into the edge of the water (the Jordan overflows all its banks throughout the harvest season), the water flowing down from upstream stopped. It rose up in a single heap a great distance away, at Adam, the town next to Zarethan, while the water running down to the Sea of the Arabah, the Dead Sea, was cut off completely. And the people crossed over opposite Jericho. The priests who bore the ark of the covenant of the LORD took a firm stand on dry ground in the middle of the Jordan. Meanwhile all Israel went across on dry ground, until the entire nation had completed the crossing.

fields.title: Joshua 4
fields.body_html:
Twelve stones from the Jordan

When the entire nation had finished its crossing of the Jordan, the LORD said to Joshua, “Choose twelve men from the people, one man from each tribe. Then command them, ‘Pick up twelve stones from here in the middle of the Jordan, from the very spot where the priests have been standing firm. Carry them over with you, and set them down at the place where you camp tonight.’”

So Joshua called together the twelve men he had chosen from the Israelites, one from each tribe. Joshua said to them, “Go ahead of the ark of the LORD your God, out to the middle of the Jordan. Every one of you is to lift a stone onto his shoulder, one for each of the tribes of the Israelites, so that this will be a sign among you. In time to come, when your children ask, ‘What do these stones mean to you?’ then tell them, ‘In front of the ark of the covenant of the LORD the waters of the Jordan were cut off. As it passed into the Jordan, the Jordan’s waters were cut off.’ These stones will be a memorial for the Israelites forever.” The Israelites did as Joshua commanded. They lifted twelve stones out of the middle of the Jordan, one for each of the tribes of the Israelites, as the LORD had told Joshua. They took them across to the camping place and laid them down there. In the middle of the Jordan, Joshua also set up twelve stones, at the spot where the priests carrying the ark of the covenant had stood. They are there to this day. The priests who carried the ark kept standing in the middle of the Jordan until everything was done that the LORD had commanded Joshua to tell the people, just as Moses had commanded Joshua. And the people crossed over in haste. When all the people had finished crossing, the ark of the LORD and the priests crossed over in front of the people. The Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh went across armed for battle, ahead of the Israelites, as Moses had told them. About 40,000 men equipped for war crossed over before the LORD, ready for battle, to the plains of Jericho.

That day the LORD raised Joshua up in the sight of all Israel, and they held him in awe all his life, just as they had held Moses in awe.

The stones set up at Gilgal

The LORD said to Joshua, “Order the priests carrying the ark of the testimony to come up from the Jordan.” So Joshua commanded the priests, “Come up out of the Jordan.” As the priests who carried the ark of the covenant of the LORD stepped up from the middle of the Jordan, and the soles of their feet came out onto dry ground, the Jordan’s waters went back to their place and flowed over all its banks as they had before. On the tenth day of the first month the people came up out of the Jordan and camped at Gilgal, on Jericho’s eastern border. Joshua set up at Gilgal the twelve stones they had taken from the Jordan. Then he said to the Israelites, “In time to come, when your children ask their parents, ‘What do these stones mean?’ then explain it to your children: ‘Israel crossed this Jordan on dry ground.’ For the LORD your God dried up the Jordan’s waters ahead of you until you had crossed, just as the LORD your God had done to the Red Sea, drying it up ahead of us until we had crossed, so that all the peoples of the earth may know how mighty the hand of the LORD is, and so that you may fear the LORD your God for all time.”

fields.title: Joshua 5
fields.body_html:
The kings west of the Jordan hear

All the kings of the Amorites west of the Jordan and all the kings of the Canaanites along the sea heard how the LORD had made the waters of the Jordan dry up ahead of the Israelites until they had crossed. When they heard it, their hearts melted, and no spirit was left in them to face the Israelites.

Circumcision at the Hill of Foreskins

At that time the LORD said to Joshua, “Make knives of flint and once more circumcise the sons of Israel, a second time.” So Joshua made knives of flint, and at the Hill of Foreskins he circumcised the sons of Israel. This is why Joshua circumcised them: all the people who came out of Egypt, the males, every man of fighting age, had died in the wilderness on the way after they left Egypt. All the people who came out had been circumcised, but none of the people born in the wilderness on the journey after leaving Egypt had been circumcised. For forty years the Israelites traveled in the wilderness, until that whole nation, the men of war who had come out of Egypt, had perished, because they had not listened to the voice of the LORD. The LORD swore to them that they would not see the land he had promised their fathers on oath to give us, a land flowing with milk and honey. It was their sons, whom he raised up in their place, that Joshua circumcised. They were uncircumcised, because no one had circumcised them on the way. When the circumcising of the whole nation was finished, they stayed where they were in the camp until they had healed.

Passover at Gilgal

Then the LORD said to Joshua, “Today I have rolled away from you the disgrace of Egypt.” So that place is called Gilgal to this day. While the Israelites were camped at Gilgal, they kept the Passover in the evening of the fourteenth day of the month, on the plains of Jericho. On the day after the Passover, that very day, they ate some of the produce of the land: unleavened bread and roasted grain. The manna stopped on the day after they ate from the produce of the land. The Israelites had no more manna; that year they ate from the crops of the land of Canaan.

The commander of the army of the LORD

Once, when Joshua was close to Jericho, he looked up, and there in front of him stood a man with his sword drawn in his hand. Joshua went over to him and asked, “Are you on our side, or on the side of our enemies?” “Neither,” he answered. “I am the commander of the army of the LORD, and now I have come.” Then Joshua threw himself down with his face to the ground and bowed low. He said to him, “What does my lord wish to say to his servant?” The commander of the army of the LORD said to Joshua, “Take the sandals off your feet. The place you are standing on is holy.” And Joshua did so.

fields.title: Joshua 6
fields.body_html:
Jericho shut up tight

Now Jericho was shut up tight because of the Israelites. Nobody left the city and nobody entered it.

Marching around the city

Then the LORD said to Joshua, “Look, I have handed Jericho over to you, along with its king and its strong warriors. All your fighting men are to march around the city, going around it once. Do this for six days. Seven priests are to carry seven rams’ horns in front of the ark. On the seventh day you are to march around the city seven times, with the priests blowing the horns. When they sound a long blast on the ram’s horn and you hear the sound of the horn, all the people are to give a great shout. Then the city wall will collapse where it stands, and the people will go up into the city, each of them straight ahead.” So Joshua son of Nun summoned the priests and said to them, “Lift up the ark of the covenant. Seven priests are to go ahead of the ark of the LORD, carrying seven rams’ horns.” And he told the people, “Go forward and march around the city, with the armed men going on ahead of the ark of the LORD.” As soon as Joshua had spoken to the people, the seven priests carrying the seven rams’ horns before the LORD went forward blowing the horns, with the ark of the covenant of the LORD coming after them. The armed men went on ahead of the priests who were sounding the horns, and the rear guard came behind the ark, with the horns sounding without a break. Joshua had given the people this order: “Do not shout. Do not let your voices be heard. Not a word is to leave your mouths until the day I tell you, ‘Shout!’ Then you will shout.” So he had the ark of the LORD taken around the city, circling it once. Then they came back to the camp and spent the night there.

The wall collapses and Rahab is spared

Joshua got up early the next morning, and the priests took up the ark of the LORD. The seven priests carrying the seven rams’ horns went on in front of the ark of the LORD, blowing the horns as they walked. The armed men went ahead of them, and the rear guard came behind the ark of the LORD, with the horns sounding without a break. On the second day they marched around the city once and went back to the camp. They did this for six days. On the seventh day they got up at daybreak and marched around the city in the same way, but this time seven times. That was the only day they went around the city seven times. The seventh time around, when the priests sounded the horns, Joshua said to the people, “Shout! The LORD has handed the city over to you. The city and everything in it are to be devoted to the LORD for destruction. Only Rahab the prostitute is to be spared, she and everyone with her in her house, because she hid the messengers we sent. But as for you, keep away from the things devoted to destruction. Do not devote them and then take any of them for yourselves. If you do, you will make the camp of Israel something devoted to destruction, and you will bring trouble on it. All the silver and gold and everything made of bronze and iron is holy to the LORD. It must go into the LORD’s treasury.” So the people shouted, and the horns were blown. As soon as the people heard the sound of the horn, they raised a great shout, and the wall collapsed where it stood. The people went up into the city, each of them straight ahead, and they took the city. They devoted to destruction everything in the city: men and women, young and old, and cattle, sheep and donkeys too. They put them all to the sword. Joshua gave an order to the two men who had spied out the land: “Go to the prostitute’s house and bring out the woman and everyone who belongs to her, just as you promised her with an oath.” So the young men who had been spies went in and brought out Rahab, with her father and mother, her brothers, and all who belonged to her. They brought out all her relatives and settled them outside the camp of Israel. Then they burned the city with fire, and everything in it. But they put the silver and gold and the bronze and iron goods into the treasury of the LORD’s house. But Joshua spared the life of Rahab the prostitute, along with her father’s household and everyone who belonged to her, and she has lived among the people of Israel to this day, because she hid the messengers Joshua had sent to spy out Jericho.

A curse on whoever rebuilds Jericho

At that time Joshua put the people under this oath: “Cursed before the LORD be the man who sets out to rebuild this city, Jericho! At the price of his firstborn he will lay its foundation; at the price of his youngest he will set its gates in place.” So the LORD was with Joshua, and his fame spread through the whole land.

fields.title: Joshua 7
fields.body_html:
Breaking faith over the devoted things

But the Israelites broke faith over the devoted things. Achan son of Carmi, son of Zabdi, son of Zerah, from the tribe of Judah, took a share of the devoted things, and the anger of the LORD burned against the Israelites. Joshua sent men from Jericho to Ai, which lies near Beth-aven, east of Bethel. He told them, “Go up and scout the land.” So the men went up and scouted out Ai. They came back to Joshua and said to him, “There is no need for all the people to go up. Let about 2,000 or 3,000 men go up and attack Ai. Do not wear out the whole army with the climb, because the people of Ai are few.” So about 3,000 of the people went up there, but they ran away from the men of Ai. The men of Ai killed about thirty-six of them. They chased them from outside the city gate as far as Shebarim and struck them down on the slope. The people lost heart; their courage melted like water. Joshua tore his clothes and fell face down on the ground before the ark of the LORD, and he stayed there until evening, he and the elders of Israel. They threw dust on their heads. Then Joshua said, “Oh, Lord GOD, why did you ever bring this people across the Jordan, only to hand us over to the Amorites to destroy us? If only we had been willing to stay on the other side of the Jordan! Please, Lord, what can I say now that Israel has turned and run from its enemies? The Canaanites and everyone who lives in the land will hear of it. They will surround us and wipe our name off the earth. Then what will you do for your great name?”

Achan is found out

The LORD said to Joshua, “Get up! Why are you lying face down like this? Israel has sinned. They have broken my covenant, which I commanded them to keep. They have taken some of the devoted things. They have stolen, they have lied, and they have put the things among their own belongings. That is why the Israelites cannot stand up to their enemies. They turn and run from them, because they themselves have become devoted to destruction. I will not be with you any longer unless you destroy the devoted things that are among you. Get up and consecrate the people. Tell them, ‘Consecrate yourselves for tomorrow, because the LORD, the God of Israel, says this: “There are devoted things among you, Israel. You cannot stand up to your enemies until you remove the devoted things from among you.” In the morning you are to come forward tribe by tribe. The tribe that the LORD picks out is to come forward clan by clan. The clan that the LORD picks out is to come forward household by household, and the household that the LORD picks out is to come forward man by man. The one who is picked out with the devoted things is to be burned, he and everything he has, because he has broken the covenant of the LORD and has done a shameful thing in Israel.’” Joshua rose early the next morning and brought Israel forward by tribes. The tribe of Judah was picked out. He brought forward the clans of Judah, and the Zerahite clan was picked out. He brought forward the Zerahite clan man by man, and Zabdi was picked out. He had Zabdi’s household come forward man by man, and Achan son of Carmi, son of Zabdi, son of Zerah, of the tribe of Judah, was picked out. Then Joshua said to Achan, “My son, give glory now to the LORD, the God of Israel. Make your confession to him. Tell me what you have done. Do not hide anything from me.” Achan answered Joshua, “It is true. I am the one who sinned against the LORD, the God of Israel. Here is what I did: Among the spoil I saw a beautiful cloak from Babylonia, about 5 pounds of silver, and a bar of gold weighing about 1 1/4 pounds. I coveted them and took them, and now they are buried in the ground in the middle of my tent. The silver is at the bottom.” So Joshua sent messengers, and they ran to the tent. There it was, hidden in his tent, with the silver underneath. They took the things out of the tent, brought them to Joshua and all the Israelites, and laid them out before the LORD. Then Joshua, and all Israel with him, seized Achan son of Zerah, together with the silver, the cloak and the gold bar, his sons and daughters, his cattle, donkeys and sheep, his tent, and all that he owned, and they led them up to the Valley of Achor. Joshua said, “Why have you brought trouble on us? The LORD will bring trouble on you today.” Then all Israel stoned him; they burned them with fire and stoned them with stones. They raised a large pile of stones over him, which is there to this day. Then the LORD turned from his burning anger. That is why the place has been called the Valley of Achor ever since.

fields.title: Joshua 8
fields.body_html:
An ambush against Ai

Then the LORD said to Joshua, “Do not be afraid or lose heart. Take the whole army with you and go up against Ai. See, I have handed the king of Ai over to you, with his people, his city and his land. Do to Ai and its king what you did to Jericho and its king, except that this time you may take its spoil and its livestock as plunder for yourselves. Set an ambush behind the city.” So Joshua and the whole army set out to go up against Ai. Joshua chose 30,000 of his best fighting men and sent them off at night. He gave them these orders: “Listen. You are to lie in wait against the city from behind it. Do not go very far from the city, and all of you be ready. I will advance on the city with all the troops who are with me. When its men march out to fight us, just as before, we will turn and run from them. They will come after us until we have drawn them away from the city, because they will think, ‘They are running from us just as before.’ So we will keep running from them. Then you will rise from your hiding place and seize the city. The LORD your God will hand it over to you. As soon as you have taken the city, set it on fire. Do what the LORD has said. Those are my orders to you.” Then Joshua sent them off. They went to their hiding place and waited between Bethel and Ai, to the west of Ai, while Joshua spent that night with the army. Early the next morning Joshua mustered the troops, and he and the elders of Israel led them up to Ai. All the fighting men with him went up, drew near and arrived in front of the city. They camped north of Ai, with the valley between them and the town. He took about 5,000 men and posted them in ambush between Bethel and Ai, west of the city. So the troops took their positions: the main camp north of the city and the rear guard west of it. That night Joshua went down into the middle of the valley. When the king of Ai saw this, he and all his people, the men of the city, hurried out early to meet Israel in battle at the place set for it, facing the Arabah. He did not know that an ambush was waiting for him behind the city. Joshua and all Israel pretended to be beaten by them and fled toward the wilderness. All the people in Ai were called out to chase them. They pursued Joshua and were drawn away from the city. Not one man stayed behind in Ai or Bethel; every one of them went out after Israel. They left the city wide open as they chased Israel.

Ai is taken

Then the LORD said to Joshua, “Hold out the javelin in your hand toward Ai, for I will hand the city over to you.” So Joshua held out the javelin in his hand toward the city. As soon as he held out his hand, the men in ambush rose quickly from their position and ran forward. They entered the city, captured it and quickly set it on fire. The men of Ai looked back and saw the smoke of their city rising into the sky. They had no chance to escape in any direction, and the Israelites who had been running toward the wilderness turned around against their pursuers. Joshua and all Israel saw the smoke going up from the city and knew that the ambush had captured it. Then they turned back and attacked the men of Ai. The men of the ambush came out of the city against them, so the men of Ai were caught in the middle, with Israelites on both sides. Israel struck them down until not one survivor or fugitive was left. But they seized the king of Ai alive and led him to Joshua. When Israel had finished killing all the people of Ai in the open country and in the wilderness where they had chased them, and every one of them had fallen by the sword until none were left, all Israel went back to Ai and put it to the sword. On that day 12,000 fell, men and women alike, the whole population of Ai. Joshua did not lower the hand that held out his javelin until he had devoted all the people of Ai to destruction. Israel kept for themselves only the livestock and the spoil of that city, as the LORD had commanded Joshua. So Joshua burned Ai and left it a ruin mound for all time, a desolate place, as it still is today. He hung the king of Ai on a tree until evening. At sunset Joshua gave the order, and they took the body down from the tree and threw it down at the entrance of the city gate. They raised over it a large heap of stones, which is there to this day.

An altar on Mount Ebal

Then Joshua built an altar to the LORD, the God of Israel, on Mount Ebal, following the command that Moses the servant of the LORD had given the Israelites, as the book of the law of Moses records: an altar of uncut stones that no iron tool had touched. On it they offered burnt offerings to the LORD and sacrificed peace offerings. There, in the presence of the Israelites, Joshua wrote on the stones a copy of the law of Moses. All Israel, with its elders, officials and judges, stood on both sides of the ark, facing the Levitical priests who carried the ark of the covenant of the LORD. Outsiders stood there as well as native Israelites. Half of them stood facing Mount Gerizim and half facing Mount Ebal. Moses the servant of the LORD had commanded this earlier, so that the people of Israel would be blessed. After that, Joshua read aloud all the words of the law, the blessing and the curse, just as they are written in the book of the law. There was not a single word of all that Moses had commanded that Joshua did not read aloud before the whole assembly of Israel, including the women and children and the outsiders who lived among them.

fields.title: Joshua 9
fields.body_html:
The kings join forces

When all the kings west of the Jordan heard of this, the kings in the hill country, in the western foothills and all along the coast of the Great Sea as far as Lebanon, the kings of the Hittites, Amorites, Canaanites, Perizzites, Hivites and Jebusites, they joined forces to make war on Joshua and Israel with one purpose.

The cunning of the Gibeonites

But when the people of Gibeon heard what Joshua had done to Jericho and Ai, they also turned to cunning. They set out posing as envoys, with worn-out sacks on their donkeys and old wineskins, cracked and tied up, with old, patched sandals on their feet and worn-out clothes on their backs. All the bread they had brought for food was dry and crumbling. So they came to Joshua in the camp at Gilgal and told him and the men of Israel, “We have come from a far-off country. Now make a treaty with us.” But the men of Israel said to the Hivites, “Perhaps you live among us. How then could we make a treaty with you?” They said to Joshua, “We are your servants.” Joshua asked them, “Who are you? Where do you come from?” They answered, “Your servants have come from a very distant country because of the fame of the LORD your God. We have heard the reports about him and all that he did in Egypt, and everything he did to the two Amorite kings east of the Jordan: Sihon, king of Heshbon, and Og, king of Bashan, whose city was Ashtaroth. So our elders and everyone who lives in our country told us, ‘Take food with you for the journey. Go and meet them and say to them, “We are your servants. Now make a treaty with us.”‘ This bread of ours was still warm when we took it from our homes as food for the road, the day we set out to come to you. Look at it now: it is dry and crumbling. These wineskins were new when we filled them, and see how they have cracked. And these clothes and sandals of ours have worn out on the long, long road.” The men of Israel took some of their provisions, but they did not seek the word of the LORD. So Joshua made peace with them and made a treaty with them to spare their lives, and the leaders of the congregation swore an oath to them. Three days after they had made the treaty with them, the Israelites heard that these people were their neighbors and were living among them. So the Israelites set out and came to their towns on the third day. Their towns were Gibeon, Chephirah, Beeroth and Kiriath-jearim. But the Israelites did not strike them down, since the congregation’s leaders had sworn to them by the LORD, the God of Israel. And the entire congregation grumbled against them. But all the leaders said to the whole congregation, “We swore an oath to them by the LORD, the God of Israel, so now we may not touch them. This is what we will do with them: we will let them live, so that no wrath comes on us because of the oath we swore to them.” The leaders told them, “Let them live.” So they became woodcutters and water carriers for the whole congregation, as the leaders had said. Then Joshua summoned them and said, “Why did you deceive us by telling us, ‘We live very far away from you,’ when in fact you live right among us? So now you are under a curse: you will never cease to be slaves, cutting wood and drawing water for the house of my God.” They answered Joshua, “Your servants were told for certain that the LORD your God had ordered Moses, his servant, to give you the whole land and to wipe out all its people before you. So we were terrified for our lives because of you, and that is why we did this. Now look, we are in your hands. Treat us in whatever way you think good and right.” So Joshua did this for them: he rescued them from the power of the Israelites, so that they did not put them to death. That day Joshua made them woodcutters and water carriers for the congregation and for the altar of the LORD at the place he would choose, and so they are to this day.

fields.title: Joshua 10
fields.body_html:
Five kings attack Gibeon

News reached Adoni-Zedek king of Jerusalem that Joshua had taken Ai and devoted it to destruction, treating Ai and its king as he had treated Jericho and its king. He also learned that the inhabitants of Gibeon had made peace with Israel and were now living among them, he and his people were terrified, because Gibeon was an important city, like one of the royal cities; it was bigger than Ai, and its men were all warriors. So Adoni-Zedek king of Jerusalem sent this message to Hoham king of Hebron, Piram king of Jarmuth, Japhia king of Lachish and Debir king of Eglon: “Come up and help me, and let us attack Gibeon, because it has made peace with Joshua and the Israelites.” Then the five Amorite kings, the kings of Jerusalem, Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish and Eglon, joined forces. They went up with all their armies, camped against Gibeon and attacked it. The men of Gibeon sent word to Joshua at the camp at Gilgal: “Do not abandon your servants! Come up to us quickly. Rescue us and help us, because all the Amorite kings of the hill country have joined forces against us.” So Joshua went up from Gilgal with his whole army, including all his best fighting men.

The LORD fights for Israel

The LORD said to Joshua, “Do not be afraid of them. I have handed them over to you. Not one of them will be able to stand against you.” Joshua marched all night from Gilgal and came upon them by surprise. The LORD threw them into panic before Israel and struck them with a great defeat at Gibeon. He chased them along the road that climbs to Beth-horon and struck them down all the way to Azekah and Makkedah. As they fled before Israel down the slope from Beth-horon, the LORD hurled huge stones on them from the sky all the way to Azekah, and they died. More of them died from the hailstones than the Israelites killed with the sword.

Sun, stand still at Gibeon

On the day the LORD gave the Amorites up to the Israelites, Joshua spoke to the LORD. In full view of Israel he said, “Sun, stand still at Gibeon, and moon, in the valley of Aijalon!” So the sun stood still, and the moon halted, until the nation had taken vengeance on its enemies. Is this not written in the Book of Jashar? The sun stopped in the middle of the sky and did not hurry to set for about a whole day. No day before it or after it has been like it, a day when the LORD listened to a man’s voice in this way. Truly the LORD fought for Israel.

The five kings in the cave at Makkedah

Then Joshua returned to the camp at Gilgal, and all Israel with him. Meanwhile the five kings had escaped and were hiding in the cave at Makkedah. Joshua was told, “The five kings have been found hiding in the cave at Makkedah.” Joshua said, “Roll large stones over the mouth of the cave, and post men there to guard the kings. But the rest of you, do not stop. Chase your enemies and cut down those at the rear. Do not let them reach their cities, because the LORD your God has handed them over to you.” When Joshua and the Israelites had finished striking them down in a very great slaughter, until they were wiped out, though a few survivors escaped into the fortified cities, the whole army came back safely to Joshua at the camp at Makkedah. No one dared to say a word against the Israelites. Then Joshua said, “Open the mouth of the cave and bring me those five kings.” They did so. They brought the five kings out of the cave to him: the kings of Jerusalem, Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish and Eglon. When they had brought these kings out to Joshua, he called for all the men of Israel. He told the commanders of the soldiers who had gone with him, “Come forward and put your feet on the necks of these kings.” So they came forward and placed their feet on their necks. Joshua said to them, “Do not be afraid or discouraged. Be strong and courageous, because this is what the LORD will do to all the enemies you fight.” After this Joshua struck them down and put them to death, and he hung them on five trees. They stayed hanging on the trees until evening. At sunset Joshua gave the order, and they took the bodies down from the trees and threw them into the cave where the kings had hidden. They placed large stones over the mouth of the cave, and they remain there to this very day.

The cities of the south are taken

Joshua captured Makkedah that same day. He struck it down with the sword, together with its king, and devoted them to destruction with everyone in it. He left no survivors. He did to the king of Makkedah what he had done to the king of Jericho. Next Joshua advanced from Makkedah to Libnah with all Israel and attacked Libnah. The LORD handed it and its king over to Israel as well. He struck it down with the sword, with everyone in it. He left no survivors. He did to its king what he had done to the king of Jericho.

Next Joshua advanced from Libnah to Lachish with all Israel. He camped against it and attacked it. The LORD handed Lachish over to Israel, and he captured it on the second day. He struck it down with the sword, with everyone in it, just as he had done to Libnah.

At that time Horam king of Gezer came up to help Lachish, but Joshua defeated him and his army, leaving him no survivors. Next Joshua advanced from Lachish to Eglon with all Israel. They camped against it and attacked it. They captured it that same day and struck it down with the sword. He devoted everyone in it to destruction that day, just as he had done to Lachish.

Next Joshua went up from Eglon to Hebron with all Israel and attacked it. They captured it and struck it down with the sword, together with its king, its towns and everyone in it. He left no survivors, just as he had done to Eglon. He devoted it to destruction with everyone in it.

Next Joshua turned back to Debir with all Israel and attacked it. He captured it, its king and all its towns. They struck them down with the sword and devoted everyone in it to destruction. He left no survivors. He did to Debir and its king what he had done to Hebron, and what he had done to Libnah and its king. So Joshua struck the whole land: the hill country, the Negev, the foothills and the slopes, with all their kings. He left no survivors. He devoted to destruction everything that breathed, as the LORD the God of Israel had commanded. Joshua struck them down from Kadesh-barnea to Gaza, and across the whole land of Goshen as far as Gibeon. Joshua captured all these kings and their land in a single campaign, because the LORD the God of Israel fought for Israel. Then Joshua returned to the camp at Gilgal, and all Israel with him.

fields.title: Joshua 11
fields.body_html:
The kings of the north

When Jabin king of Hazor heard of this, he sent word to Jobab king of Madon, to the king of Shimron, to the king of Achshaph, and to the kings of the north, those in the hill country, in the Arabah south of Chinneroth, in the foothills, and in the heights of Dor to the west, to the Canaanites in the east and the west, to the Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites and Jebusites in the hill country, and to the Hivites below Mount Hermon in the region of Mizpah. They came out with all their forces, an army as countless as the sand along the seashore, with a great many horses and chariots. All these kings joined forces; they came and camped together at the waters of Merom to fight against Israel.

Victory over the northern kings

The LORD said to Joshua, “Have no fear of them. At this hour tomorrow I will lay every one of them dead before Israel. You are to hamstring their horses and set fire to their chariots.” So Joshua and all his fighting men came upon them suddenly at the waters of Merom and attacked them. The LORD handed them over to Israel, who defeated them and chased them to Great Sidon and Misrephoth-maim, and toward the east to the valley of Mizpeh. They kept striking them down until not one was left. Joshua did to them just as the LORD had told him: he hamstrung their horses and set fire to their chariots.

Hazor is burned

At that time Joshua came back and took Hazor; he put its king to the sword, for Hazor had once been the leading power among all these kingdoms. They put everyone in it to the sword, devoting them to destruction, and no one who breathed was left. Then Joshua burned Hazor. Joshua captured all the towns of these kings, and their kings as well, and put them to the sword. He devoted them to destruction, just as Moses the servant of the LORD had commanded. But Israel did not burn any of the towns that stood on their mounds, except Hazor alone, which Joshua burned. The Israelites took all the spoil of these towns and the livestock for themselves. But every human being they killed with the sword until they had wiped them out; they left no one alive. Just as the LORD had commanded his servant Moses, so Moses had commanded Joshua, and that is what Joshua did. He left nothing undone of all that the LORD had commanded Moses. So Joshua took this whole land: the hill country, all the Negev, all the land of Goshen, the foothills, the Arabah, and the hill country of Israel with its foothills, from Mount Halak, rising toward Seir, to Baal-gad in the Lebanon valley below Mount Hermon. He captured all their kings, struck them down and put them to death. Joshua waged war against all these kings for a long time. Not one town made peace with the Israelites except the Hivites who lived in Gibeon. All the others they took in battle. For it was the LORD who made their hearts stubborn, so that they came out to meet Israel in battle, in order that they would be devoted to destruction and receive no mercy, but be wiped out, just as the LORD had commanded Moses.

The Anakim wiped out

At that time Joshua went and wiped out the Anakim from the hill country: from Hebron, Debir and Anab, and from the whole hill country of Judah and of Israel. He devoted them to destruction together with their towns. In the land of the Israelites no Anakim were left; some remained only in Gaza, Gath and Ashdod. So Joshua took the entire land, just as the LORD had told Moses, and he gave it to Israel as an inheritance, divided among their tribes. And the land had peace from war.

fields.title: Joshua 12
fields.body_html:
The kings defeated east of the Jordan

These are the kings of the land whom the Israelites defeated and whose land they took possession of across the Jordan, toward the sunrise, from the Arnon Valley to Mount Hermon, with all the Arabah on the east: Sihon king of the Amorites, whose city was Heshbon. His rule reached from Aroer, on the edge of the Arnon Valley, and from the middle of the valley, over half of Gilead as far as the Jabbok River, the border of the Ammonites. He also ruled the Arabah on the east, from the Sea of Chinneroth down to the Sea of the Arabah, the Dead Sea, in the direction of Beth-jeshimoth, and southward below the slopes of Pisgah. They also took the territory of Og king of Bashan, one of the last of the Rephaim, who lived at Ashtaroth and Edrei. He ruled over Mount Hermon, Salecah and all of Bashan, up to the border of the Geshurites and the Maacathites, and over half of Gilead, up to the border of Sihon king of Heshbon. Moses the servant of the LORD and the Israelites defeated them, and Moses the servant of the LORD gave their land as a possession to the Reubenites, the Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh.

The kings defeated west of the Jordan

These are the kings of the land whom Joshua and the Israelites defeated across the Jordan on the west side, from Baal-gad in the Lebanon Valley up to Mount Halak, the mountain that rises toward Seir. Joshua gave their land to the tribes of Israel as a possession, portion by portion, in the hill country and the foothills, in the Arabah and on the slopes, in the wilderness and in the Negev, the land of the Hittites, the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Perizzites, the Hivites and the Jebusites.

The king of Jericho, one; the king of Ai, which is near Bethel, one; the king of Jerusalem, one; the king of Hebron, one; the king of Jarmuth, one; the king of Lachish, one; the king of Eglon, one; the king of Gezer, one; the king of Debir, one; the king of Geder, one; the king of Hormah, one; the king of Arad, one; the king of Libnah, one; the king of Adullam, one; the king of Makkedah, one; the king of Bethel, one; the king of Tappuah, one; the king of Hepher, one; the king of Aphek, one; the king of Lasharon, one; the king of Madon, one; the king of Hazor, one; the king of Shimron-meron, one; the king of Achshaph, one; the king of Taanach, one; the king of Megiddo, one; the king of Kedesh, one; the king of Jokneam in Carmel, one; the king of Dor in Naphath-dor, one; the king of Goiim in Gilgal, one; the king of Tirzah, one. Thirty-one kings in all.

fields.title: Joshua 13
fields.body_html:
Very much of the land still remains

Joshua had now grown old, far along in years. The LORD said to him, “You have grown old and are far along in years, and very much of the land still remains to be taken. This is the land that remains: all the regions of the Philistines and all the land of the Geshurites, from the Shihor east of Egypt as far north as the border of Ekron, which is counted as Canaanite land. There are the five rulers of the Philistines, those of Gaza, Ashdod, Ashkelon, Gath and Ekron, and there are the Avvim, from the south, all the land of the Canaanites, and Mearah, which belongs to the Sidonians, as far as Aphek and the border of the Amorites; and the land of the Gebalites, and the whole of Lebanon toward the sunrise, from Baal-gad below Mount Hermon to Lebo-hamath; all who live in the hill country from Lebanon as far as Misrephoth-maim, all the Sidonians. I am the one who will drive them out before the Israelites. Only allot the land to Israel as an inheritance, as I have commanded you. So now divide this land as an inheritance for the nine tribes and the half-tribe of Manasseh.” With the other half of Manasseh, the Reubenites and the Gadites had received their inheritance, which Moses gave them east of the Jordan, as Moses the servant of the LORD had assigned it to them, from Aroer on the edge of the Arnon Valley, and the town in the middle of the valley, and all the plateau of Medeba as far as Dibon, and all the towns of Sihon king of the Amorites, who reigned in Heshbon, up to the Ammonite border, and Gilead, and the territory of the Geshurites and the Maacathites, all Mount Hermon, and all Bashan as far as Salecah, the whole kingdom of Og in Bashan, who reigned in Ashtaroth and Edrei. He was one of the last survivors of the Rephaim. Moses defeated them and drove them out. But the Israelites did not drive out the Geshurites and the Maacathites, so Geshur and Maacath live among Israel to this day. Only to the tribe of Levi he gave no inheritance. The food offerings of the LORD, the God of Israel, are its inheritance, as he promised it.

The land of Reuben

Moses gave land to the tribe of the descendants of Reuben, clan by clan. Their territory ran from Aroer on the edge of the Arnon Valley, with the town in the middle of the valley and all the plateau by Medeba, Heshbon and all its towns on the plateau: Dibon, Bamoth-baal, Beth-baal-meon, Jahaz, Kedemoth, Mephaath, Kiriathaim, Sibmah, Zereth-shahar on the hill in the valley, Beth-peor, the slopes of Pisgah, and Beth-jeshimoth, all the towns of the plateau, and the whole kingdom of Sihon king of the Amorites, who reigned in Heshbon. Moses had defeated him and the leaders of Midian, Evi, Rekem, Zur, Hur and Reba, the princes allied with Sihon who lived in the land. The Israelites also killed Balaam son of Beor, who practiced divination, with the sword, along with the others they killed. The Jordan and its banks formed the border of the Reubenites. This was the inheritance of the descendants of Reuben, clan by clan, the towns and their villages.

The land of Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh

Moses gave land to the tribe of Gad, to the descendants of Gad, clan by clan. Their territory was Jazer and all the towns of Gilead, and half the land of the Ammonites, up to Aroer east of Rabbah, and from Heshbon up to Ramath-mizpeh and Betonim, and from Mahanaim up to the border of Debir, and in the valley, Beth-haram, Beth-nimrah, Succoth and Zaphon, what remained of the kingdom of Sihon king of Heshbon, with the Jordan as its border up to the end of the Sea of Chinnereth, on the east side of the Jordan. This was the inheritance of the descendants of Gad, clan by clan, the towns and their villages. Moses gave land to the half-tribe of Manasseh. It belonged to half the tribe of the descendants of Manasseh, clan by clan. Their territory reached from Mahanaim through all Bashan, the whole kingdom of Og king of Bashan, with all the villages of Jair in Bashan, sixty towns, and half of Gilead, with Ashtaroth and Edrei, the royal towns of Og in Bashan. These were given to the descendants of Machir son of Manasseh, to half of the descendants of Machir, clan by clan. These are the inheritances Moses gave out in the plains of Moab, across the Jordan from Jericho, to the east.

But to the tribe of Levi Moses gave no inheritance. The LORD, the God of Israel, is their inheritance, as he promised them.

fields.title: Joshua 14
fields.body_html:
Dividing the inheritance in Canaan

These are the lands that the Israelites received as their inheritance in the land of Canaan. Eleazar the priest, Joshua son of Nun and the family heads of the tribes of Israel assigned these lands to them. Their inheritance was assigned by lot, as the LORD had commanded through Moses, for the nine and a half tribes. Moses had already given the two and a half tribes their inheritance east of the Jordan, but he did not give the Levites an inheritance among the others. The descendants of Joseph had become two tribes, Manasseh and Ephraim. The Levites were given no share of the land, only towns to live in, with the pasturelands around them for their flocks and herds. The Israelites did just as the LORD had commanded Moses, and they divided up the land.

Caleb receives Hebron

The men of Judah came to Joshua at Gilgal. Caleb son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite spoke to him: “You know what the LORD told Moses the man of God at Kadesh-barnea concerning you and me. When Moses the servant of the LORD sent me out from Kadesh-barnea to explore the land, I was forty years old. I brought him back a report that was true to what was in my heart. My companions who went up with me made the people lose heart, but I followed the LORD my God with all my heart. On that day Moses swore an oath: ‘The land where you have set foot will surely be an inheritance for you and your descendants for all time, because you have followed the LORD my God with all your heart.’ Now the LORD has kept me alive, just as he promised, for these forty-five years since he said this to Moses, while Israel journeyed in the wilderness. And here I am today, eighty-five years old. Today I am just as strong as on the day Moses sent me. My strength now is what it was then, for war and for going out and coming in. So now give me this hill country, the one the LORD promised me on that day. You yourself heard then that the Anakim were there, with large fortified cities. Perhaps the LORD will be with me, and I will drive them out, just as the LORD said.” Joshua blessed him and gave Hebron to Caleb son of Jephunneh as his inheritance. So Hebron has belonged to Caleb son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite as his inheritance to this day, because he followed the LORD, the God of Israel, with all his heart. Hebron used to be called Kiriath-arba, after Arba, who was the greatest man among the Anakim. Then the land had peace from war.

fields.title: Joshua 15
fields.body_html:
The borders of Judah

The land that fell by lot to the tribe of Judah, clan by clan, reached south to the border of Edom and the wilderness of Zin, at the far southern end. Their southern border ran from the end of the Dead Sea, from the bay that faces south. It goes out south of the Ascent of Akrabbim, passes along to Zin, goes up south of Kadesh-barnea, passes Hezron, goes up to Addar and turns toward Karka, passes Azmon, and goes out to the Wadi of Egypt, ending at the sea. This will be your southern border. On the east, the Dead Sea forms the border, up to the mouth of the Jordan. On the north side the border begins at the bay where the Jordan enters the sea. The border goes up to Beth-hoglah and passes north of Beth-arabah, then goes up to the Stone of Bohan son of Reuben. From the Valley of Achor the border goes up to Debir and turns north toward Gilgal, which faces the Ascent of Adummim, on the south side of the wadi. It goes on to the waters of En-shemesh and comes out at En-rogel. Then the border goes up the Valley of Ben-hinnom along the southern slope of the Jebusite city, that is, Jerusalem. From there it goes up to the hilltop that looks across the Valley of Hinnom from the west, at the northern end of the Valley of Rephaim. From the top of the hill the border curves around to the spring of the waters of Nephtoah, goes out to the towns of Mount Ephron, and bends around to Baalah, that is, Kiriath-jearim. From Baalah the border turns west to Mount Seir, passes along the northern slope of Mount Jearim, that is, Chesalon, then goes down to Beth-shemesh and on to Timnah. The border goes out to the slope north of Ekron, curves around to Shikkeron, passes along to Mount Baalah and goes out to Jabneel. It ends at the sea. The western border is the Great Sea and its coast. These are the borders of the people of Judah on every side, clan by clan. Caleb son of Jephunneh was given a share among the people of Judah, as the LORD had commanded Joshua. It was Kiriath-arba, that is, Hebron. Arba was the father of Anak. Caleb drove out from there the three sons of Anak, Sheshai, Ahiman and Talmai, the descendants of Anak. From there he went up against the people who lived in Debir. Debir used to be called Kiriath-sepher. Caleb said, “I will give my daughter Achsah as a wife to the man who attacks Kiriath-sepher and captures it.” Othniel son of Kenaz, Caleb’s brother, captured it, so Caleb gave him his daughter Achsah as his wife. When she came to Othniel, she urged him to ask her father for a field. As she got down from her donkey, Caleb asked her, “What do you want?” She answered, “Give me a gift. Because the land you have given me is in the Negev, give me springs of water too.” So Caleb gave her the upper springs and the lower springs.

The towns of Judah

This is the inheritance of the tribe of Judah, clan by clan. The towns at the far end of the tribe of Judah, toward the border of Edom in the Negev, were Kabzeel, Eder, Jagur, Kinah, Dimonah, Adadah, Kedesh, Hazor, Ithnan, Ziph, Telem, Bealoth, Hazor-hadattah, Kerioth-hezron (that is, Hazor), Amam, Shema, Moladah, Hazar-gaddah, Heshmon, Beth-pelet, Hazar-shual, Beer-sheba, Biziothiah, Baalah, Iim, Ezem, Eltolad, Chesil, Hormah, Ziklag, Madmannah, Sansannah, Lebaoth, Shilhim, Ain and Rimmon: in all, twenty-nine towns and their villages.

Towns in the foothills

In the foothills: Eshtaol, Zorah, Ashnah, Zanoah, En-gannim, Tappuah, Enam, Jarmuth, Adullam, Socoh, Azekah, Shaaraim, Adithaim, Gederah and Gederothaim: fourteen towns and their villages. Zenan, Hadashah, Migdal-gad, Dilean, Mizpeh, Joktheel, Lachish, Bozkath, Eglon, Cabbon, Lahmas, Chitlish, Gederoth, Beth-dagon, Naamah and Makkedah: sixteen towns and their villages.

Libnah, Ether, Ashan, Iphtah, Ashnah, Nezib, Keilah, Achzib and Mareshah: nine towns and their villages.
