Ekron with its towns and villages; from Ekron west to the sea, all the towns near Ashdod, with their villages; Ashdod with its towns and villages, and Gaza with its towns and villages, as far as the Wadi of Egypt and the coast of the Great Sea.

Towns in the hill country

In the hill country: Shamir, Jattir, Socoh, Dannah, Kiriath-sannah (that is, Debir), Anab, Eshtemoh, Anim, Goshen, Holon and Giloh: eleven towns and their villages. Arab, Rumah, Eshan, Janum, Beth-tappuah, Aphekah, Humtah, Kiriath-arba (that is, Hebron) and Zior: nine towns and their villages.

Maon, Carmel, Ziph, Juttah, Jezreel, Jokdeam, Zanoah, Kain, Gibeah and Timnah: ten towns and their villages. Halhul, Beth-zur, Gedor, Maarath, Beth-anoth and Eltekon: six towns and their villages. Kiriath-baal (that is, Kiriath-jearim) and Rabbah: two towns and their villages.

Towns in the wilderness

In the wilderness: Beth-arabah, Middin, Secacah, Nibshan, the City of Salt and En-gedi: six towns and their villages. But the people of Judah could not drive out the Jebusites, who lived in Jerusalem, and the Jebusites live there with the people of Judah to this day.

fields.title: Joshua 16
fields.body_html:
The land of Joseph’s descendants

The allotment for the descendants of Joseph ran from the Jordan at Jericho, east of the springs of Jericho, through the wilderness that climbs from Jericho up into the hill country to Bethel. From Bethel it goes on to Luz and passes along to Ataroth, in the territory of the Archites. Then it goes down westward to the territory of the Japhletites, as far as the territory of Lower Beth-horon, and on to Gezer, and it ends at the sea. So the descendants of Joseph, Manasseh and Ephraim, received their inheritance. This was the territory of the Ephraimites, clan by clan. The border of their inheritance ran on the east from Ataroth-addar to Upper Beth-horon, and out to the sea. From Michmethath on the north the border turns east toward Taanath-shiloh and passes by it on the east to Janoah. From Janoah it goes down to Ataroth and Naarah, reaches Jericho, and comes out at the Jordan. From Tappuah the border goes west along the Wadi Kanah and ends at the sea. This is the inheritance of the Ephraimite tribe, clan by clan, together with the towns set apart for the Ephraimites within the inheritance of the Manassites, all those towns and their villages. But they did not drive out the Canaanites living in Gezer, and so Canaanites have lived among the Ephraimites to this day, though they were made to work as forced laborers.

fields.title: Joshua 17
fields.body_html:
The land of Manasseh

This was the land that came by lot to the tribe of Manasseh, for he was Joseph’s firstborn. Machir, Manasseh’s firstborn and the father of Gilead, had Gilead and Bashan, because he was a warrior. The lot was also for the rest of Manasseh’s descendants, clan by clan: the clans of Abiezer, Helek, Asriel, Shechem, Hepher and Shemida. These were the male descendants of Manasseh son of Joseph, listed by their clans. But Zelophehad son of Hepher, son of Gilead, son of Machir, son of Manasseh, had no sons, only daughters. His daughters were named Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah and Tirzah. They came forward before Eleazar the priest, Joshua son of Nun and the leaders. “The LORD commanded Moses,” they said, “to give us an inheritance among our relatives.” So Joshua gave them an inheritance among their father’s brothers, as the LORD had commanded. So ten shares fell to Manasseh, besides the land of Gilead and Bashan across the Jordan, because the daughters of Manasseh received an inheritance along with his sons. The land of Gilead belonged to the rest of Manasseh’s descendants. The border of Manasseh ran from Asher to Michmethath, east of Shechem. From there the border goes south toward the people of En-tappuah. The land around Tappuah belonged to Manasseh, but the town of Tappuah itself, on Manasseh’s border, belonged to the descendants of Ephraim. Then the border goes down to the Wadi Kanah. South of the wadi there were towns that belonged to Ephraim, though they lay among the towns of Manasseh. Manasseh’s border runs along the north side of the wadi and ends at the sea. The land to the south belonged to Ephraim and the land to the north to Manasseh, with the sea as its border. Manasseh reaches Asher on the north and Issachar on the east. In the land of Issachar and Asher, Manasseh also had Beth-shean, Ibleam, and the people of Dor, En-dor, Taanach and Megiddo, each with its villages: the three hill districts. But the descendants of Manasseh could not take over these towns, because the Canaanites were determined to stay in that land. Later, when the Israelites had grown stronger, they made the Canaanites do forced labor, but they never drove them out completely.

Joseph’s descendants ask for more land

Joseph’s descendants asked Joshua, “Why have you given us just one allotment, a single share, as our inheritance? We are a large people, because the LORD has blessed us until now.” Joshua answered them, “If you are so many, go up into the forest and clear land for yourselves there, in the land of the Perizzites and the Rephaim, since the hill country of Ephraim is too small for you.” The descendants of Joseph replied, “The hill country is too small for us, and the Canaanites who live down in the valley all have iron chariots, both those in Beth-shean and its villages and those in the Valley of Jezreel.” Then Joshua answered the house of Joseph, Ephraim and Manasseh: “You are a large people and you have great strength. You will not have just one allotment, but the hill country will be yours as well. It is forest, but you will clear it, and it will be yours to its farthest edges. You will drive out the Canaanites, even though they have iron chariots and are strong.”

fields.title: Joshua 18
fields.body_html:
Describing the rest of the land at Shiloh

The whole congregation of the Israelites gathered at Shiloh, and there they pitched the tent of meeting. The land now lay subdued before them. But among the Israelites there were still seven tribes that had not been given their inheritance. So Joshua said to the Israelites, “How long will you hold back from going in to take possession of the land that the LORD, the God of your ancestors, has given you? Choose three men from each tribe, and I will send them out. They are to set out and go through the land, write a description of it with a view to dividing it as their inheritance, and then come back to me. They are to divide it into seven portions. Judah will keep its territory in the south, and the house of Joseph will keep theirs in the north. You are to describe the land in seven portions and bring the description here to me. Then here, before the LORD our God, I will cast lots for you. The Levites have no portion among you, because the priesthood of the LORD is their inheritance. And Gad, Reuben and the half-tribe of Manasseh already have their inheritance east of the Jordan, the land that Moses the servant of the LORD gave them.” So the men set out. As they were going to describe the land, Joshua gave them this command: “Go through the land, write a description of it, and come back to me. Then here in Shiloh, before the LORD, I will cast lots for you.” The men went and traveled through the land. They described it town by town in seven portions, writing it in a scroll, and came back to Joshua at the camp in Shiloh. Joshua cast lots for them in Shiloh in the presence of the LORD, and there he divided the land among the Israelites, giving each tribe its portion.

The land of Benjamin

The first lot came up for the tribe of Benjamin, clan by clan. The territory that fell to them lay between the people of Judah and the people of Joseph. On the north side their border started at the Jordan. It goes up the slope north of Jericho, climbs westward through the hill country and comes out at the wilderness of Beth-aven. From there the border passes on toward Luz, along the southern slope of Luz (that is, Bethel), and goes down to Ataroth-addar, on the hill that lies south of Lower Beth-horon. Then the border bends and turns south along the western side, from the hill that faces Beth-horon on the south, and ends at Kiriath-baal (that is, Kiriath-jearim), a town belonging to the people of Judah. This is the western side. The southern side starts from the edge of Kiriath-jearim. The border goes out westward and on to the spring of the waters of Nephtoah. The border then goes down to the foot of the hill facing the Valley of Ben-hinnom, at the north end of the Valley of Rephaim. It runs down the Valley of Hinnom along the southern slope of the Jebusite city and down to En-rogel. From there it bends northward and goes out to En-shemesh, then on to Geliloth, which is opposite the Ascent of Adummim, and goes down to the Stone of Bohan son of Reuben. It passes on to the northern slope opposite the Arabah and goes down into the Arabah. The border passes on to the northern slope of Beth-hoglah and ends at the northern bay of the Dead Sea, where the Jordan flows into it at the south. This is the southern border. The Jordan forms its boundary on the east. This was the inheritance of the tribe of Benjamin, clan by clan, with its borders on every side. The towns of the tribe of Benjamin, clan by clan, were these: Jericho, Beth-hoglah, Emek-keziz, Beth-arabah, Zemaraim, Bethel, Avvim, Parah, Ophrah, Kephar-ammonah, Ophni and Geba, twelve towns and their villages. Then Gibeon, Ramah, Beeroth, Mizpeh, Chephirah, Mozah, Rekem, Irpeel, Taralah, Zelah, Haeleph, Jebus (that is, Jerusalem), Gibeah and Kiriath, fourteen towns and their villages. This was the inheritance of the tribe of Benjamin, clan by clan.

fields.title: Joshua 19
fields.body_html:
The land of Simeon

The second lot came out for the tribe of Simeon, clan by clan. Their inheritance lay inside the inheritance of the tribe of Judah. Their inheritance included Beersheba, Sheba, Moladah, Hazar-shual, Balah, Ezem, Eltolad, Bethul, Hormah, Ziklag, Beth-marcaboth, Hazar-susah, Beth-lebaoth and Sharuhen: thirteen towns and their villages, and also Ain, Rimmon, Ether and Ashan: four towns and their villages, together with all the villages around these towns, out to Baalath-beer, Ramah of the Negev. This was the inheritance of the tribe of Simeon, clan by clan. The inheritance of the tribe of Simeon came out of the share of the tribe of Judah, because Judah’s share was too large for them. So the tribe of Simeon received its inheritance inside Judah’s.

The land of Zebulun

The third lot came up for the tribe of Zebulun, clan by clan. The border of their inheritance reached as far as Sarid. Their border goes up westward to Maralah, reaches Dabbesheth, and reaches the wadi that faces Jokneam. From Sarid it turns east, toward the sunrise, to the border of Chisloth-tabor, goes on to Daberath, and goes up to Japhia. From there it goes on east, toward the sunrise, to Gath-hepher and Eth-kazin, and goes out to Rimmon, where it bends toward Neah. On the north the border goes around to Hannathon and ends at the valley of Iphtah-el. Also in it were Kattath, Nahalal, Shimron, Idalah and Bethlehem: twelve towns and their villages. This was the inheritance of the tribe of Zebulun, clan by clan: these towns and their villages.

The land of Issachar

The fourth lot came out for the tribe of Issachar, clan by clan. Their territory reached to Jezreel and included Chesulloth, Shunem, Hapharaim, Shion, Anaharath, Rabbith, Kishion, Ebez, Remeth, En-gannim, En-haddah and Beth-pazzez. The border reaches Tabor, Shahazumah and Beth-shemesh, and it ends at the Jordan: sixteen towns and their villages. This was the inheritance of the tribe of Issachar, clan by clan: the towns and their villages.

The land of Asher

The fifth lot came out for the tribe of Asher, clan by clan. Their territory included Helkath, Hali, Beten, Achshaph, Allammelech, Amad and Mishal. On the west it reaches Carmel and Shihor-libnath. Then it turns east toward the sunrise to Beth-dagon, reaches Zebulun and the valley of Iphtah-el to the north, Beth-emek and Neiel, and goes on to Cabul on the north, Ebron, Rehob, Hammon and Kanah, as far as great Sidon. Then the border turns to Ramah and on to the fortified city of Tyre. It turns to Hosah and ends at the sea, in the district of Achzib, and also Ummah, Aphek and Rehob: twenty-two towns and their villages. This was the inheritance of the tribe of Asher, clan by clan: these towns and their villages.

The land of Naphtali

The sixth lot came out for the tribe of Naphtali, clan by clan. Their border runs from Heleph, from the great tree at Zaanannim, by Adami-nekeb and Jabneel as far as Lakkum, and it ends at the Jordan. Then the border turns west to Aznoth-tabor and goes on from there to Hukkok. It reaches Zebulun on the south and Asher on the west, and on the east it reaches Judah at the Jordan. The fortified towns were Ziddim, Zer, Hammath, Rakkath, Chinnereth, Adamah, Ramah, Hazor, Kedesh, Edrei, En-hazor, Iron, Migdal-el, Horem, Beth-anath and Beth-shemesh: nineteen towns and their villages. This was the inheritance of the tribe of Naphtali, clan by clan: the towns and their villages.

The land of Dan

The seventh lot came out for the tribe of Dan, clan by clan. The territory of their inheritance included Zorah, Eshtaol, Ir-shemesh, Shaalabbin, Aijalon, Ithlah, Elon, Timnah, Ekron, Eltekeh, Gibbethon, Baalath, Jehud, Bene-berak, Gath-rimmon, Me-jarkon and Rakkon, with the territory facing Joppa. But the territory of the Danites was lost to them, so the Danites went up and fought against Leshem. They captured it, put it to the sword, took possession of it, and settled there. They renamed Leshem Dan, after their ancestor Dan. This was the inheritance of the tribe of Dan, clan by clan: these towns and their villages.

An inheritance for Joshua

When they had finished dividing up the land as inheritances by its borders, the Israelites gave Joshua son of Nun an inheritance among them. At the command of the LORD they gave him the town he asked for, Timnath-serah in the hill country of Ephraim. He built up the town and settled there. Eleazar the priest, Joshua son of Nun, and the family heads of the tribes of the Israelites handed out these inheritances by lot at Shiloh, before the LORD at the entrance of the tent of meeting. So they finished dividing the land.

fields.title: Joshua 20
fields.body_html:
Cities of refuge

Then the LORD said to Joshua, “Tell the Israelites: ‘Appoint the cities of refuge that I told you about through Moses, so that anyone who kills a person by mistake, without meaning to, can flee there. They will be a place of refuge for you from the avenger of blood. The one who killed is to flee to one of these cities, stand at the entrance of the city gate and explain the case to the elders of that city. Then they are to take that person into the city and give them a place to live among them. If the avenger of blood comes after them, the elders must not hand the killer over to the avenger, because the killer struck the neighbor without meaning to and had not been that neighbor’s enemy before. The killer is to stay in that city until standing trial before the congregation, and until the death of the high priest who is serving at that time. Then the killer may go back home to their own city and their own house, the city they fled from.’” So they set apart these cities: Kedesh in Galilee, in the hill country of Naphtali; Shechem, in the hill country of Ephraim; and Kiriath-arba, which is Hebron, in the hill country of Judah. East of the Jordan, across from Jericho, they assigned Bezer in the wilderness on the plateau, from the tribe of Reuben; Ramoth in Gilead, from the tribe of Gad; and Golan in Bashan, from the tribe of Manasseh. These were the cities designated for all the Israelites and for the outsiders living among them. Anyone who killed a person by mistake could flee there and not die at the hands of the avenger of blood before standing trial before the congregation.

fields.title: Joshua 21
fields.body_html:
Towns for the Levites

The family heads of the Levites came to Eleazar the priest, to Joshua son of Nun and to the family heads of the tribes of Israel. They spoke to them at Shiloh in the land of Canaan and said, “The LORD commanded through Moses that we be given towns to live in, and their pasturelands for our livestock.” So at the command of the LORD, the Israelites gave the Levites the following towns and their pasturelands out of their own inheritance. The lot came out for the clans of the Kohathites. The descendants of Aaron the priest, who were among the Levites, received thirteen towns by lot from the tribes of Judah, Simeon and Benjamin.

The rest of the descendants of Kohath received ten towns by lot from the clans of the tribe of Ephraim, from the tribe of Dan and from the half-tribe of Manasseh.

The descendants of Gershon received thirteen towns by lot from the clans of the tribe of Issachar, from the tribes of Asher and Naphtali and from the half-tribe of Manasseh in Bashan.

The descendants of Merari, clan by clan, received twelve towns from the tribes of Reuben, Gad and Zebulun. So the Israelites gave these towns and their pasturelands to the Levites by lot, as the LORD had commanded through Moses.

The towns of Aaron’s descendants

From the tribes of Judah and Simeon they gave the towns that are named below. They went to the descendants of Aaron, who belonged to the Kohathite clans among the Levites, because the first lot fell to them. They gave them Kiriath-arba (Arba was the father of Anak), that is, Hebron, in the hill country of Judah, and its pasturelands around it. But the fields of the town and its villages they had already given to Caleb son of Jephunneh as his own property.

To the descendants of Aaron the priest they gave the city of refuge for anyone who had killed someone, Hebron and its pasturelands, along with Libnah and its pasturelands, Jattir and its pasturelands, Eshtemoa and its pasturelands, Holon and its pasturelands, Debir and its pasturelands, Ain and its pasturelands, Juttah and its pasturelands, and Beth-shemesh and its pasturelands. These were nine towns from these two tribes.

From the tribe of Benjamin they gave Gibeon and its pasturelands, Geba and its pasturelands, Anathoth and its pasturelands, and Almon and its pasturelands: four towns. In all, the descendants of Aaron, the priests, received thirteen towns and their pasturelands.

The towns of the other Kohathite clans

As for the rest of the Kohathite clans of the Levites, the towns allotted to them were from the tribe of Ephraim. They gave them the city of refuge for anyone who had killed someone, Shechem and its pasturelands in the hill country of Ephraim, along with Gezer and its pasturelands, Kibzaim and its pasturelands, and Beth-horon and its pasturelands: four towns.

From the tribe of Dan they gave Elteke and its pasturelands, Gibbethon and its pasturelands, Aijalon and its pasturelands, and Gath-rimmon and its pasturelands: four towns.

From the half-tribe of Manasseh they gave Taanach and its pasturelands, and Gath-rimmon and its pasturelands: two towns. In all, the rest of the Kohathite clans received ten towns and their pasturelands.

The towns of Gershon’s descendants

To the descendants of Gershon, one of the Levite clans, they gave from the half-tribe of Manasseh the city of refuge for anyone who had killed someone, Golan in Bashan and its pasturelands, and Beeshterah and its pasturelands: two towns.

From the tribe of Issachar they gave Kishion and its pasturelands, Daberath and its pasturelands, Jarmuth and its pasturelands, and En-gannim and its pasturelands: four towns.

From the tribe of Asher they gave Mishal and its pasturelands, Abdon and its pasturelands, Helkath and its pasturelands, and Rehob and its pasturelands: four towns.

From the tribe of Naphtali they gave the city of refuge for anyone who had killed someone, Kedesh in Galilee and its pasturelands, along with Hammoth-dor and its pasturelands, and Kartan and its pasturelands: three towns. In all, the Gershonite clans received thirteen towns and their pasturelands.

The towns of Merari’s descendants

To the clans of the descendants of Merari, the rest of the Levites, they gave from the tribe of Zebulun Jokneam and its pasturelands, Kartah and its pasturelands, Dimnah and its pasturelands, and Nahalal and its pasturelands: four towns. From the tribe of Reuben they gave Bezer and its pasturelands, Jahaz and its pasturelands, Kedemoth and its pasturelands, and Mephaath and its pasturelands: four towns.

From the tribe of Gad they gave the city of refuge for anyone who had killed someone, Ramoth in Gilead and its pasturelands, along with Mahanaim and its pasturelands, Heshbon and its pasturelands, and Jazer and its pasturelands: four towns in all. All the towns given to the descendants of Merari, clan by clan, the rest of the Levite clans, came by lot to twelve towns. In all, the Levites had forty-eight towns and their pasturelands within the land held by the Israelites. Each of these towns had its pasturelands around it; it was the same for all of these towns.

Not one good promise failed

In this way the LORD gave Israel the whole land that he had sworn to give to their ancestors, and they took possession of it and settled there. The LORD gave them rest all around them, in keeping with everything he had sworn to their ancestors. Not one of all their enemies could stand against them; the LORD handed all their enemies over to them. Of all the good promises the LORD had made to the house of Israel, not one failed; every one of them was fulfilled.

fields.title: Joshua 22
fields.body_html:
The eastern tribes sent home

Then Joshua summoned the Reubenites, the Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh. He said to them, “You have carried out all that Moses the servant of the LORD commanded you, and in everything I have commanded you, you have obeyed me. All this long time, up to this very day, you have not abandoned your fellow Israelites. You have faithfully carried out the duty that the LORD your God commanded. Now the LORD your God has given your fellow Israelites rest, as he promised them. So turn now and go home to your tents, to the land that is your own, which Moses the servant of the LORD gave you on the other side of the Jordan. But take great care to carry out the commandment and the law which Moses the servant of the LORD laid on you: love the LORD your God, walk in all his ways, keep his commandments, hold fast to him, and serve him with all your heart and all your soul.” Then Joshua blessed them and sent them off, and they went home to their tents.

Moses had given one half of the tribe of Manasseh land in Bashan; to the other half Joshua had given land west of the Jordan, beside their fellow Israelites. When Joshua sent the eastern tribes home, he blessed them and said to them, “Go back to your homes with great wealth: large herds of livestock, silver, gold, bronze and iron, and a great amount of clothing. Share the plunder taken from your enemies with your relatives at home.”

An altar by the Jordan

So the Reubenites, the Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh turned back and parted from the Israelites at Shiloh, in the land of Canaan, to go to the land of Gilead. That was their own land, which had become theirs at the command of the LORD given through Moses. When they reached the region along the Jordan that lies in the land of Canaan, the Reubenites, the Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh built an altar there by the Jordan, an altar of imposing size. Then the Israelites heard the report: “The Reubenites, the Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh have built an altar at the edge of the land of Canaan, in the region along the Jordan, on the Israelite side.” When the Israelites heard this, the whole congregation of the Israelites assembled at Shiloh to march out and fight against them.

Phinehas is sent to Gilead

So the Israelites sent Phinehas son of Eleazar the priest to the Reubenites, the Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh in the land of Gilead. With him went ten leaders, one leader from each ancestral family for every tribe of Israel. Each of them was the head of his family among the clans of Israel. They went to the land of Gilead, to the Reubenites, the Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh, and spoke with them: “The whole congregation of the LORD says this: ‘How could you commit such a breach of faith against the God of Israel? Today you have turned away from following the LORD by building yourselves an altar, rebelling against the LORD this very day. Was the sin at Peor not enough for us? To this day we have not cleansed ourselves from it, even though a plague struck the congregation of the LORD. And now you are turning away from following the LORD today! If you rebel against the LORD today, tomorrow he will be angry with the whole congregation of Israel. But if the land you possess is unclean, come over to the LORD’s own land, where the LORD’s tabernacle stands, and take a share of land among us. Only do not rebel against the LORD, and do not rebel against us, by building an altar for yourselves other than the altar of the LORD our God. When Achan son of Zerah broke faith over the devoted things, did not wrath fall on the whole congregation of Israel? He was only one man, but he was not the only one to die for his sin.’”

The eastern tribes answer

Then the Reubenites, the Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh answered the heads of the clans of Israel: “The Mighty One, God, the LORD! The Mighty One, God, the LORD! He knows, and let Israel know too! If this was rebellion or a breach of faith against the LORD, do not spare us today, if we built ourselves an altar to turn away from following the LORD, or to offer burnt offerings and grain offerings on it, or to present peace offerings on it, may the LORD himself call us to account. No, we did it because we were worried about what might happen. We thought that someday your descendants might say to ours, ‘What do you have to do with the LORD, the God of Israel? The LORD has set the Jordan as a border between us and you, you Reubenites and Gadites. You have no share in the LORD.’ In that way your descendants could make ours stop fearing the LORD. So we said, ‘Let us take action and build an altar, not for burnt offerings or for sacrifices, but to be a witness between us and you, and between the generations after us, that we are to worship the LORD in his presence by bringing our burnt offerings, sacrifices and peace offerings. So your descendants will never be able to say to ours in days to come, “You have no share in the LORD.”‘ We said, ‘If that is ever said to us or to our descendants, our answer will be, “Look at this copy of the altar of the LORD, which our ancestors made. It is not for burnt offerings or sacrifices. It is a witness between us and you.”‘ Far be it from us to rebel against the LORD and to stop following the LORD today by building an altar for burnt offerings, grain offerings or sacrifices apart from the altar of the LORD our God that stands in front of his tabernacle.”

A witness between us

When Phinehas the priest and the leaders of the congregation, the heads of the clans of Israel who were with him, heard what the Reubenites, the Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh said, they were satisfied. Phinehas son of Eleazar the priest said to the Reubenites, the Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh, “Today we know that the LORD is in our midst, since you have not broken faith with the LORD in this way. By this you have rescued the Israelites from the hand of the LORD.” Then Phinehas son of Eleazar the priest and the leaders left the Reubenites and the Gadites in the land of Gilead and returned to the land of Canaan, to the Israelites, and gave them their report. The report pleased the Israelites, and they praised God. They did not speak again of going to war against them to lay waste the land where the Reubenites and the Gadites lived. The Reubenites and the Gadites named the altar Witness, “because,” they said, “it stands as a witness between us that the LORD is God.”

fields.title: Joshua 23
fields.body_html:
Joshua’s charge to the leaders of Israel

A long time afterward, when the LORD had given Israel rest from every enemy on all sides, and Joshua was old and well along in years, Joshua called together all Israel, their elders, leaders, judges and officials, and said to them, “I am now old and well along in years. You yourselves have seen everything the LORD your God has done to all these nations on your account. It is the LORD your God himself who has been fighting for you. Look, I have given out to you by lot the land of these nations that remain, as an inheritance for your tribes, together with the land of all the nations I have already destroyed, from the Jordan to the Great Sea in the west. The LORD your God himself will push them back ahead of you and drive them out of your way, and you will take possession of their land, just as the LORD your God has promised you. So be very strong, and keep and carry out everything written in the book of the law of Moses, without turning aside from it to the right or to the left, so that you do not mix with these nations that are left among you. Do not even speak the names of their gods, or make anyone swear by them. Do not serve them or bow down to them. Instead, hold fast to the LORD your God, as you have done up to now. The LORD has driven out great and powerful nations ahead of you, and to this day no one has been able to stand against you. One of your men can put a thousand to flight, because the LORD your God himself fights for you, as he promised you. So be very careful, for your own sake, to love the LORD your God. For if you ever turn away and attach yourselves to what is left of these nations that remain among you, if you intermarry with them and mix with them and they with you, you can be sure that the LORD your God will no longer drive these nations out ahead of you. They will become a trap and a snare for you, a whip on your sides and thorns in your eyes, until you are wiped out from this good land the LORD your God has given you. Now I am about to go the way of all the earth. You know with your whole heart and your whole being that not a single word has fallen short of all the good words the LORD your God spoke about you. Every one has come to pass for you; not one word of it has fallen short. But just as every good thing that the LORD your God promised you has come to you, so the LORD will bring on you every evil thing he has threatened, until he has destroyed you and you are gone from this good land that the LORD your God has given you. If you break the covenant of the LORD your God, which he laid on you, and go off to serve other gods and bow down to them, the anger of the LORD will blaze against you, and you will quickly be wiped out from the good land he has given you.”

fields.title: Joshua 24
fields.body_html:
The tribes gathered at Shechem

Joshua gathered all the tribes of Israel at Shechem. He called for the elders of Israel, its leaders, its judges and its officers, and they took their stand before God. Then Joshua told all the people, “The LORD, the God of Israel, says this: ‘In ancient times your ancestors lived on the far side of the River, Terah, father of Abraham and of Nahor, and they served other gods. But I took your father Abraham from the far side of the River and led him all through the land of Canaan. I made his descendants many, and I gave him Isaac. To Isaac I gave Jacob and Esau. I gave Esau the hill country of Seir as his own, but Jacob and his sons went down to Egypt. I sent Moses and Aaron, and I struck Egypt with plagues by what I did among its people. After that I brought you out. When I brought your ancestors out of Egypt and you reached the sea, the Egyptians chased after your ancestors with chariots and horsemen as far as the Red Sea. Then they cried out to the LORD, and he set darkness between you and the Egyptians. He brought the sea over them, and it covered them. You saw with your own eyes what I did in Egypt. Then you lived in the wilderness for a long time. I brought you into the land of the Amorites who lived east of the Jordan. They fought against you, but I handed them over to you. You took their land as your own, and I wiped them out ahead of you. Then Balak son of Zippor, king of Moab, rose up and made war on Israel. He sent for Balaam son of Beor to put a curse on you. But I would not listen to Balaam. Instead he blessed you over and over, and I rescued you from his power. Then you crossed the Jordan and came to Jericho. The leading citizens of Jericho fought against you, and so did the Amorites, Perizzites, Canaanites, Hittites, Girgashites, Hivites and Jebusites, but I handed them over to you. I sent the hornet ahead of you, and it drove them out before you, the two Amorite kings. It was not your sword or your bow that did it. I gave you a land you had not worked for and towns you had not built, and you live in them. You eat from vineyards and olive groves you did not plant.’ So now, fear the LORD and serve him with a whole heart and with faithfulness. Remove from among you the gods your ancestors served across the River and in Egypt, and serve the LORD. If serving the LORD seems wrong to you, then make your choice today. Whom will you serve? The gods your ancestors served beyond the River, or the gods of the Amorites, whose land you now live in? My household and I will serve the LORD.”

We will serve the LORD

The people answered, “We would never abandon the LORD to serve other gods! It is the LORD our God who brought us and our ancestors up from the land of Egypt, from the house of slavery. He did these great signs before our eyes, and he kept us safe all along the road we traveled and among all the peoples we passed through. The LORD drove out all the peoples ahead of us, including the Amorites who lived in the land. So we too will serve the LORD, because he is our God.”

A covenant at Shechem

Joshua said to the people, “You will not be able to serve the LORD, because he is a holy God, a jealous God; he will not pardon your rebellion and your sins. If you leave the LORD and serve the gods of foreigners, he will turn against you. He will bring harm on you and put an end to you, after all the good he has done you.” But the people said to Joshua, “No! We will serve the LORD.” Then Joshua said to the people, “You are your own witnesses that you have chosen the LORD for yourselves and will serve him.” They answered, “We are witnesses.” “Then remove the foreign gods that are among you,” he said, “and turn your hearts to the LORD, the God of Israel.” And the people told Joshua, “It is the LORD our God we will serve, and it is his voice we will obey.” So Joshua made a covenant for the people that day, and at Shechem he laid down a statute and a ruling for them. Joshua wrote these words in the book of God’s law. He also took a great stone and raised it there under the oak that stood near the sanctuary of the LORD.

A stone as a witness

Joshua said to all the people, “See this stone? It will stand as a witness against us, for it has heard every word the LORD said to us. It will be a witness against you, so that you do not deny your God.” Then Joshua sent the people away, each to their own inheritance.

The death of Joshua

After these events, Joshua son of Nun, the servant of the LORD, died, at 110 years of age. They buried him within the borders of his own inheritance, at Timnath-serah, north of Mount Gaash in the hill country of Ephraim. Israel served the LORD all through Joshua’s lifetime, and through the lifetime of the elders who lived on after him and had known for themselves every work that the LORD had done for Israel. The bones of Joseph, which the Israelites had brought up from Egypt, were buried at Shechem, in the piece of ground that Jacob had bought from the sons of Hamor, Shechem’s father, paying a hundred pieces of silver. It became part of the inheritance of Joseph’s descendants. Eleazar son of Aaron died too. They buried him at Gibeah, the hill town of his son Phinehas, which had been given to Phinehas in the hill country of Ephraim.

fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
Israel served the LORD all through Joshua’s lifetime, and through the lifetime of the elders who lived on after him and had known for themselves every work that the LORD had done for Israel.

— Joshua 24:31

Joshua ends with three graves. Joshua himself is buried at Timnath-serah, in the hill country he was given. Eleazar the priest, Aaron’s son, is buried in the hill country of Ephraim. And between them, almost in passing, the book records the burial of a man who had died centuries before: “The bones of Joseph, which the Israelites had brought up from Egypt, were buried at Shechem.” The last request of Genesis has been honoured. The promise that kept Joseph’s bones waiting in Egypt has come true.

The question the book leaves with you

And yet the book ends with a sentence that has a shadow in it. Israel served the LORD as long as Joshua lived, and as long as the elders lived who had seen what God had done. What happens when they are gone?

Joshua had seen the danger. He set up stones at the Jordan so that children would ask what they meant. He warned the people that they would not be able to serve a holy God by their own resolve. He wrote the covenant in a book and raised a stone to witness it. The very next book gives the answer he feared: “after them another generation grew up who did not know the LORD or what he had done for Israel.”

That is the question Joshua leaves with every reader. Faith cannot be inherited like a field. Each generation has to choose, and each generation has to be told. Joshua’s “My household and I will serve the LORD” is not only a vow for himself. It is a charge to every parent, every church, every elder who has seen the works of God, to make sure the next generation sees them too.

The rest still waiting

The book says that “the LORD gave them rest all around them”, and that not one of his good promises failed. But it also says that much of the land was never taken, and the books that follow tell how Israel lost even what it had. The rest Joshua gave was real, and it did not last.

The New Testament reads that as a signpost. The letter to the Hebrews, noting that long after Joshua, God still says through David, “Today, if you hear his voice”, draws the conclusion:

“If Joshua had brought them into rest, God would not afterward speak of a different day. So a Sabbath rest is still waiting for God’s people.”

— Hebrews 4:8–9

There is a deeper Joshua, and a deeper rest. The Christian church has always heard something in the fact that Jesus bears Joshua’s name, “the LORD saves”, and that he too leads his people across a river, through death, into an inheritance. And it has noticed who was waiting on the far side: Rahab, the Canaanite who trusted the God of Israel, is named in Matthew’s first chapter among the ancestors of Jesus.

Where to go from here

Joshua has been read in the church as a story of faith, of courage, and of the Christian life, and some of the best of that reading is in this library. A few places to begin:

  • On the whole book. Hannah Whitall Smith’s Old Testament Types and Teachings, whose chapter “Joshua: Heavenly Places” reads the entry into the land, beside Ephesians, as a picture of the believer’s victories “in heavenly places” in Christ; and Justin Martyr’s Dialogue with Trypho, whose chapter “Joshua was a figure of Christ” is one of the earliest Christian readings of the book.
  • On Rahab (Joshua 2 and 6). Clement of Rome’s The First Epistle of Clement to the Corinthians, whose twelfth chapter tells her story and sees the scarlet cord as a sign of redemption through the Lord’s blood; and the chapter “Rahab” in Gareth Evans’s He Holds My Tomorrows, on Hebrews 11:31.
  • On Jericho (Joshua 6). Hannah Whitall Smith’s chapter “The Shout of Faith” in The God of All Comfort, on Joshua 6:5.
  • On Achan and Ai (Joshua 7). Andrew Murray’s chapter “Restraining Prayer—Is It Sin?” in The Ministry of Intercession, which reads the defeat at Ai as a lesson in hidden sin and restored blessing.
  • On Caleb (Joshua 14). Alexander Maclaren’s sermon Caleb—A Green Old Age (Joshua 14:6–14), and Gareth Evans’s sermon Caleb: A Different Spirit, which moves from Numbers 14:24 to Caleb’s request for Hebron.
  • On the choice at Shechem (Joshua 24). George Whitefield’s sermon “The Great Duty of Family Religion”, on Joshua 24:15, in Selected Sermons of George Whitefield.
  • On the rest still waiting. Richard Baxter’s The Saints’ Everlasting Rest, a whole book on Hebrews 4:9.
  • For reading with children. “Into the Land”, on Joshua 1–6 and 24, in The Big Story, an Ochorus Original.

You can also go the other way, from the text to the classics. Every reference to Joshua in this library can be tapped to read the verse, and the Scripture pages gather, chapter by chapter, what the great writers of the church have said about each passage of this book.

And then read on into Judges, which begins with the words “After Joshua died”, and tells what came of the choice at Shechem. But before you turn the page, the question Joshua asked is worth answering for yourself:

If serving the LORD seems wrong to you, then make your choice today. Whom will you serve? The gods your ancestors served beyond the River, or the gods of the Amorites, whose land you now live in? My household and I will serve the LORD.”

— Joshua 24:15
